endorsements.title: Implementing Artificial Intelligence in Radiology: Design Thinking Road Map
endorsements.quote: Measurable clinical and operational benefits should be quantified, as even tools with excellent performance may fail to deliver real-world value depending on the specific context in which they are deployed [ 51 ].

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence and Enhanced Recovery After Surgery as Patient Safety Strategies for Perioperative Care in Resource-Limited Settings
endorsements.quote: Tools should be locally validated, clinically supervised, and judged not only by algorithmic performance but also by their effect on postoperative complications, recovery, cost, workflow, staff trust, and equity.

evidence.title: Impact of the National Early Warning Score-based sepsis response system on hospital-onset sepsis in a tertiary hospital in South Korea
evidence.effect: The SRP group had a lower 30-day mortality risk (hazard ratio, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.36-0.86; P=0.017) than the preliminary group.
evidence.quote: The SRP group showed a lower 30-day mortality risk (hazard ratio, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.36-0.86; P=0.017) compared to the preliminary group.

evidence.title: Pharmacist-led surgical medicines prescription optimization and prediction service improves patient outcomes - a machine learning based study
evidence.outcome: Clinical outcomes and costs after AI deployment
evidence.effect: After implementing the AI-assisted service, recommendation acceptance rose to 71.30%, median length of stay dropped to 7 days, and both total and medication costs decreased significantly.
evidence.quote: Compared to the ML development period and external validation period, the acceptance rate of pharmacists’ recommendations in the post-implementation evaluation period increased from 40.63% to 71.30%, the length of stay was reduced from 13 days (IQR: 8, 22) ( P < 0.001) to 7 days (IQR: 9, 15) ( p < 0.001), total hospitalization costs decreased from 32,263.42 RMB (IQR: 16,880.46,68,921.29) ( p < 0.001) to 20,842.89 RMB (IQR: 13,516.59, 32,055.51) ( p < 0.001), cost of medication decreased from 7847.67 RMB (IQR: 3815.45,19,980.16) ( p < 0.001) to 4,712.92 RMB (IQR: 2866.63, 7716.55) ( p < 0.001), and the ADR rate was reduced from 0.4% to 0.18% ( p = 0.095).

evidence.title: Implementation costs and cost-effectiveness of ultraportable chest X-ray with artificial intelligence in active case finding for tuberculosis in Nigeria
evidence.effect: AI combined with symptom screening detected more cases at US$773 per case, whereas cough-only screening missed 60% of cases at US$1198 per case.
evidence.quote: The combined screening algorithm using both symptoms and CXR-AI detected more bacteriologically-confirmed cases at US$773 per case detected, whereas symptom-only screening criteria missed 60% cases at a much higher US$1198 per case detected cost for cough ≥ 2 weeks criteria and 10% missed cases at cost lower than CXR algorithm of US$636 per case detected.

evidence.title: Pragmatic Implementation Study of a Computer-Aided Detection Device on Colonoscopy Outcomes at a Trainee-Dominated Academic County Hospital
evidence.outcome: Adenoma and sessile serrated lesion detection rates before vs after CADe implementation
evidence.effect: ADR rose from 31.5% baseline by +7.6% (95% CI 4.6-10.6); SSLDR from 1.3% by +2.9% (95% CI 1.9-3.8); aOR 1.29 for adenoma, 3.10 for SSL detection
evidence.quote: After adjusting for other covariates (age, gender, BBPS, withdrawal time, positive fecal immunochemical test indication), the odds of adenoma detection (aOR 1.29, 95% CI 1.12-1.51, p = 0.001) and sessile serrated lesion detection (aOR 3.10, 95% CI 1.93-4.99, p < 0.001) were higher after CADe implementation.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Algorithms Improve Care of Patients with AAA
evidence.effect: 42% of patients received initial evaluation post-AI compared to 18% pre-AI.
evidence.quote: A greater proportion of patients underwent initial AAA evaluation after implementation of AI-assisted AAA care (42% vs. 18%, P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Hemodialysis equipment malfunction incidence and risk profiling in clinical settings: a retrospective single-center cohort analysis
evidence.effect: Predictive model-guided interventions reduced total alarm frequency by 43%, false alarms by 56%, response time by 38%, and treatment interruptions by 51%.
evidence.quote: Implementation of model-guided interventions resulted in substantial improvements across all key performance indicators: 43% reduction in total alarm frequency ( P < 0.001), 56% reduction in false alarm rate ( P < 0.001), 38% improvement in response time ( P < 0.001), and 51% reduction in treatment interruptions ( P < 0.001).

evidence.title: The Implementation of a Clinical Decision Support System for Managing Drug-Disease Interactions in Outpatients with Cardiovascular and Diabetic Comorbidities: An Interventional Study at a Tertiary Hospital in Vietnam
evidence.effect: The rate of relative contraindication dropped from 0.33% to 0.01% after deployment of the system.
evidence.quote: The rate of relative contraindication plummeted from 0.33% to 0.01% (P < 0.05).

evidence.title: Utilizing standardized nursing terminologies in implementing an AI-powered fall-prevention tool to improve patient outcomes: a multihospital study
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: longitudinal fall rates and nurse interventions
evidence.effect: no significant fall rate decrease (-1.21 to 0.21) but intervention rates increased
evidence.quote: There was no significant longitudinal decrease in the fall rate (P = .160, 95% CI = -1.21 to 0.21 per 1000 hospital days), but rates of interventions provided by nurses were notably increased.

evidence.title: Impact of an Alert-Based Inpatient Clinical Decision Support Tool to Prevent Drug-Induced Long QT Syndrome: Large-Scale, System-Wide Observational Study
evidence.effect: the risk of diLQTS was not significantly different, and mortality was significantly higher after deployment
evidence.quote: When compared with rates prior to implementation, the risk of diLQTS was not significantly different after the CDS tools were deployed across the system, although mortality was significantly higher after the tools were implemented.

commentary.bottom_line: Seven deployment studies quantified local outcomes after AI rollout and all reported favorable changes, but five used before-after designs without comparison groups, and none tested whether documenting and measuring outcomes changes decisions to deploy or retain tools. Two quasi-experimental studies found no benefit and, in one, higher mortality after deployment, which suggests local outcome measurement may reveal results that model performance alone would not.

perspectives.view: Five of seven studies are pre-post designs without comparators. One is a quasi-experimental study of 352 patients that reported a hazard ratio of 0.56 for 30-day mortality, and one compared screening costs. All seven evaluated the tools rather than the evaluation practice, so the evidence is indirect. Uniformly favorable findings may reflect selective publication. Certainty is very low.

Two larger quasi-experimental deployments found that a fall-prediction tool raised nurse interventions without lowering falls, and that a drug-induced long QT tool was followed by higher mortality. These studies show that tools can fail or cause harm locally. They do not show that outcome documentation prevents harm, although both findings came from post-deployment measurement.

The studies suggest that outcome, safety, and cost data can be collected in real deployments across varied settings, including 3,966 colonoscopies and 4,231 alarm events. None reported the staff time, data infrastructure, or observation period the measurement required. The burden and fidelity of sustained local evaluation therefore remain unknown.

Two studies quantified costs. One reported lower total and medication costs and a median stay of 7 days after an AI-assisted prescription service. Another reported US$773 per case detected with AI plus symptom screening, compared with US$1198 for cough-only screening. Neither study reported what the evaluation itself cost.

One study screened 5,297 people in Nigeria with low health literacy. Another, in a US safety-net setting, found adenoma detection rose by 7.6% (95% CI 4.6-10.6) from a 31.5% baseline. No study reported results for Medicaid or limited English proficiency groups, and none reported outcomes stratified by population subgroup.

Two studies measured mortality. One reported lower 30-day mortality after deployment, and the other reported higher mortality. The remaining studies tracked process or safety measures such as evaluation rates, alarm counts, and contraindication rates. No study measured patient experience, trust, or access to a clinician, so patients have little evidence on how local evaluation affects their care.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared tool deployments with and without structured local outcome evaluation to learn whether measurement leads to earlier retirement of ineffective tools, fewer harms, or better cost decisions. Controlled or interrupted time-series designs would address this question if they used prespecified outcomes and reported both evaluation costs and subgroup results.
commentary.underserved_note: Two tests included underserved groups. One was a Nigerian screening program with participants of low health literacy (pmid:40498780), and the other was a US safety-net colonoscopy program (pmid:40858859). No test included Medicaid-identified or limited English proficiency populations, so it is unknown whether local evaluation captures benefits and harms for those patients.
